extracted.intended_audience: prospective students of Prof. aBa’s Math 395 (undergraduates with proof-writing background)
extracted.subtask_description: Syllabus and excerpt for Math 395 (1-credit directed studies): Part 1 is student-led presentations of beautiful proofs (from Proofs from THE BOOK); Part 2 covers permutations/combinatorics with instructor-led lectures and possible research directions. Includes logistical, prerequisite, textbook, and production instructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prerequisite: proof-writing course requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: You ABSOLUTELY need to have taken (even concurrently this Fall 2014) at least ONE of the following proof-writing courses: 314, 324, or 425.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concurrency is allowed; this is a hard prerequisite for enrollment/participation in Math 395 (Beauty of Math).

rubrics_metrics.name: Course goals
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two. First, we explore the most BEAUTIFUL proofs in mathematics. Second, we focus on combinatorial objects called permutations and study various combinatorial properties of these objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both goals are central — Part 1 addresses beautiful proofs across several areas; Part 2 focuses on permutations and related combinatorial research directions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credit & meeting time
rubrics_metrics.description: Math 395 Directed Studies Course – Fall 2014 (1 credit course meeting 1 hour per week – time & place TBD).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Course is 1 credit with a single weekly hour; logistics (time/place) to be announced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format of Part 1: student-led presentations of proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Since this is a directed studies course, we will all take part in teaching it. The plan for the 'Beauty of Mathematics' part is for each of us to take turns presenting proofs from the book Proofs from THE BOOK. This part will cover number theory, geometry, analysis, combinatorics, and graph theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students are expected to prepare and present assigned proofs; participation and peer-teaching are integral to the course format.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format of Part 2: instructor lecture then student presentations and research exploration
rubrics_metrics.description: Part 2 will start with the instructor lecturing on permutations like in a standard lecture class. Then students present material. Time-permitting, the course will explore possible directions of research that can be pursued later (next semester, summer, etc.). The instructor will brush up on background (e.g., permutation matrices, symmetric group) if missing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part 2 mixes traditional lecturing with student presentations and may include research-problem exploration; instructor supports background gaps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flexibility in course progression (caveat)
rubrics_metrics.description: There being two parts to this course does NOT mean that Part 1 takes half the semester and Part 2 is the other half. If we are having LOADS of fun with Part 1, then we can just continue presenting the most beautiful proofs. The instructor can teach Part 2 next semester if needed. If after the first two weeks everyone is bored with beautiful proofs, then we can move on to Part 2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schedule and balance between Parts 1 and 2 are determined dynamically by class interest; students should expect possible mid-course shifts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Textbooks / readings provided
rubrics_metrics.description: TEXTBOOKS: (I will provide excerpts of these for you as needed) Proofs from THE BOOK (4th Edition) by Aigner & Ziegler; Combinatorics of Permutations by Miklós Bóna; The Symmetric Group (2nd Edition) by Bruce Sagan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructor will supply excerpts as needed — purchasing entire texts may not be required; readings drawn from these sources will form the basis of presentations and lectures.

rubrics_metrics.name: PDF production / printing instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: There have been selective blank pages placed into the PDF to preserve the front and back pages as they appear in the book. So print this pdf DOUBLE-SIDED starting with pg.1 or pg.3 (if you want to start with the 'cover' of the book).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow double-sided printing starting on indicated page to preserve intended page order/cover layout.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection criterion for 'Proofs from THE BOOK' content
rubrics_metrics.description: The authors state: 'We have no definition or characterization of what constitutes a proof from The Book: all we offer here is the examples that we have selected... The selection is to a great extent influenced by Paul Erdős himself.' They also limit topics to those 'accessible to readers whose backgrounds include only a modest amount of technique from undergraduate mathematics: a little linear algebra, some basic analysis and number theory, and a healthy dollop of elementary concepts and reasonings from discrete mathematics.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection emphasizes 'beautiful' proofs (brilliant ideas, clever insights, wonderful observations) and accessibility to undergraduates with modest background; there is no formal checklist — aesthetic and accessibility considerations guide inclusion.
